title: The first sin
hook: Augustine taught that Adam's guilt is inherited; the Orthodox speak of inheriting mortality and a wounded nature, not guilt

segments.voice: Yesterday, image and likeness: the image given to every person, the likeness grown into. Your line was image given, likeness grown.

Why is it so easy to do the very thing you just decided not to do? The second cookie. The sharp reply. The phone, picked up again. In Romans, Paul writes: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Christian readers have heard more than a bad day in it: a pull in the grain of being human, there before anyone chooses it. Christians name where that pull comes from, and tell its story in more than one way. Today's word: original sin.
screen: `THE THING YOU DECIDED NOT TO DO.`
`THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.`

segments.voice: Original sin doesn't mean an unusual sin. It means the sin at the origin: Adam and Eve in the garden, reaching for the fruit, and everything that followed. Day three hundred thirteen called sin a condition everyone shares. Paul ties the story to all of us: "as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." Christian teaching, East and West, says something went wrong at the start and reached everyone. They differ on what was passed down. Augustine, the bishop in North Africa, taught that Adam's guilt itself is inherited: in Adam all humanity sinned, and every child is born sharing that guilt as well as its damage. In the West, Catholics and Protestants build on his reading, with different stresses. The Orthodox churches of the East tell it differently. What we inherit from Adam, they say, is not his guilt but mortality, and a wounded nature that leans toward sin. A newborn isn't guilty of anything, but is born into a world where death and the pull toward wrong are already in the air. Guilt, in Orthodox teaching, is for sins a person actually commits. Here's what both readings refuse to say: that a person is worthless. Before the garden, Genesis says God looked at everything he had made, "and, behold, it was very good." The fall doesn't undo that. Wounded, in every telling. Worthless, in none.

Think back over the last day, without hunting for your worst moment, and find one small place where you felt a tug you didn't want to follow: impatience, a little lie, wanting to be first. Look at it the way a doctor looks at a bruise, honestly and without disgust, and name it quietly. If you pray, hold it out to God and ask for healing; if not, let it be seen, and breathe with it.
Original sin. The sin at the origin, and what it left in us. Augustine said guilt; the Orthodox say mortality and a wounded nature.
Your line: wounded, not worthless. The wound is real, and so is the very good. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians speak of original sin when they teach about baptism and grace; Western churches build on Augustine's teaching of inherited guilt in different ways, while Orthodox churches teach that people inherit mortality and a wounded nature, not Adam's guilt.

chat.meaning: Augustine taught Adam's guilt is inherited; Orthodox teaching says we inherit mortality and a wounded nature, not guilt. Neither says a person is worthless.

notes: The Orthodox position (inherited mortality and a corrupted or wounded nature, not personal guilt) is summarized; confirm with an Orthodox Keeper. Romans 5:12's 'for that all have sinned' is read differently East and West (Augustine's Latin 'in quo', in whom); left out under the claims rule.

'In the Western churches, Catholics and Protestants build on his reading, in different ways' is a general historical claim; confirm. Catholic teaching speaks of original sin as 'contracted, not committed'; Reformed teaching stresses inherited guilt more. Not detailed here.
The 'original' note associates the Latin peccatum originale with Augustine; confirm he used the phrase (e.g., Ad Simplicianum 1.1.10) or drop the association.
Practice invites noticing without self-contempt; confirm it is suitable and does not assume the listener's beliefs.
